stories.headline: Seven Dead, More Than 100 Injured After Trains Collide Near Giza, Egypt
stories.summary:
At least seven people were killed and more than 100 injured when two passenger trains collided near the city of Giza, Egypt's railway authority said. A train traveling from Giza to Fayoum struck the rear of a stationary Cairo-to-Aswan service. Several carriages derailed and fell down an embankment, and images from the scene showed at least one carriage split in two.

The collision occurred between the Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat. The driver of one of the trains was among the dead. Egypt's health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said patients were being treated for broken bones and head injuries, and hospitals in the area were placed on heightened alert. The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise, and the Egyptian Red Crescent provided aid and psychological support at the scene.

President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered authorities to investigate and to hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent. Some in Egypt called on the transport minister to resign. Train service between Giza and Upper Egypt was suspended while cranes cleared the wreckage, and no timeline was given for reopening the line.

The crash occurred near the site of Egypt's deadliest rail disaster, a February 2002 fire on a Cairo-to-Luxor train that officially killed more than 370 people. Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more. Saudi Arabia and Turkey were among those expressing condolences.

stories.headline: Update: Iran Threatens to 'Rain Down Hell' as Trump Says Renewed Strikes Unlikely If Talks Progress
stories.summary:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned that Tehran will "rain down hell" if the United States resumes attacks, issuing what he called a two-day proposal in a post on X. "Meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results," he wrote, "or choose war." Iran's Foreign Ministry also said it would not go easy on American targets in the region. The two countries are in the eighth month of war.

President Donald Trump said in a phone interview reported by CNN that renewed strikes are "highly unlikely" if negotiations over Iran's nuclear program and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz progress. "It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," he said, adding that he would continue strikes if necessary. He said three US aircraft carriers in the region are "fully locked and loaded" and that 38 Iranian bridges are in US crosshairs.

The exchange followed Iranian state media reports that an oil tanker caught fire after hitting a naval mine east of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's navy said the ship's identification systems were off and that it was in a no-go zone. An IRGC Aerospace Force adviser, Brig. Gen. Ali Belali, said weapons have been "secured for years to come."

Araghchi said negotiations were delayed by the US midterm elections, in which Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and that it will take time before mediators resume visits. Today's development is the sharpening of rhetoric from both sides alongside the tanker incident, as diplomacy remains stalled.

stories.headline: Iran Executes Three Men Over Armed Unrest in January Protests
stories.summary:
Iran has executed three men convicted of carrying out armed unrest during January's anti-government protests, according to state media. Hassan Dioband, Hamid Kazemi and Reza Zanganeh were accused by the Tasnim news agency of throwing Molotov cocktails and grenades, using bladed weapons and firearms, and setting fire to public facilities in Karaj, west of Tehran. Damage allegedly included an electricity substation that caused power outages.

Tasnim said the executions followed the Supreme Court's upholding of their convictions for "participating in operational activities on behalf of the Israeli Zionist regime, the United States and hostile groups." Dioband was arrested on January 11, and ten others accused of taking part under his supervision were later arrested. Reuters reported they received prison terms of five to ten years.

The protests began in December over the high cost of living and grew into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on January 8 and 9. Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths and blamed US- and Israel-orchestrated "terrorist acts." Foreign-based rights groups gave higher figures, and the BBC received accounts of security forces firing on unarmed protesters.

Executions have risen since US-Israeli strikes on Iran began in late February. UN rights chief Volker Turk said in August that at least 56 people had been executed on national security charges since March 19, including 27 tied to the protests. Amnesty International says Iran put to death at least 2,159 people last year, the highest figure it has recorded since 1981.

stories.headline: Former HHS Adviser Calley Means Blames Susie Wiles and Sugar Industry Money for Stalling MAHA Agenda
stories.summary:
Calley Means, a former senior adviser at the Department of Health and Human Services, accused outgoing White House chief of staff Susie Wiles of slowing the Make America Healthy Again agenda. He made the claims in a two-hour interview with podcaster Joe Rogan. Means quit the administration less than two weeks before the midterm elections, reportedly frustrated by disputes over food policy, including delays in defining ultra-processed foods.

Means said Wiles repeatedly told him, "We need money for the midterms," and that she opposed a proposal requiring the food industry to address sugar levels in children's diets because she needed sugar industry money. He also alleged nepotism, saying companies that hired Wiles's daughter, Katie Wiles, at the lobbying firm Continental Strategy received priority in the White House. He criticized Wiles rather than HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. or President Donald Trump, though he voiced concern about special-interest influence in the administration.

The interview aired the same day Trump announced Wiles was leaving her post to join the Trump political operation, replaced by Stephen Miller. Trump praised Wiles as having done an "outstanding job." Wiles called serving Trump "the honor of a lifetime." The Washington Examiner report did not include a response from Wiles to Means's allegations. MAHA activists have welcomed her departure, while the White House has not publicly addressed the specific claims.

stories.headline: Update: US Carries Out New Limited Strikes on Iran's Air Defenses as Tehran Weighs Proposals
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said the U.S. military has carried out new limited strikes on Iran, targeting air defense systems. The Associated Press reported the strikes came as Iran's leaders weigh proposals tied to the nuclear program and negotiations over the conflict.

The strikes add a fresh military action to a confrontation that has already included a U.S. naval blockade enforcement, the creation of a special unit to block Iranian arms shipments over land routes, and a $20 million U.S. reward offer for information on Iran's nuclear program. Earlier reporting indicated that Vice President JD Vance has been leading a behind-the-scenes push for a new ceasefire and nuclear talks.

The description of the strikes as limited, and their focus on air defenses rather than other targets, suggests Washington is applying military pressure while diplomacy remains open. Details on the scale of the strikes, any casualties, and Iran's response were not available in the initial report.

What happens next depends on whether Iranian leaders accept any of the proposals under consideration and whether Tehran retaliates. The developments come amid continued reports of Iran rebuilding and digging near missile bases, which has heightened concern in Washington about the pace of its military recovery.

stories.headline: Update: Russian Strikes Hit Ukrainian Rescuers and Power Grid Ahead of Abu Dhabi Talks
stories.summary:
A Russian drone struck emergency workers on rescue missions in southern Ukraine on Sunday, hitting a former school and nearby shelter that had earlier been blasted by multiple Russian guided bombs while residents waited for humanitarian aid. Officials said at least nine 3,000-kilogram aerial bombs hit a southern Ukrainian village in an attack President Volodymyr Zelensky called "utterly horrific."

Separate Russian attacks on energy infrastructure in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions left about 850,000 people without power. Authorities said the broader attacks killed at least two people across Ukraine and wounded about a dozen others, and damaged homes, businesses and non-residential buildings.

The strikes come ahead of trilateral talks between Ukrainian and Russian delegations, with U.S. involvement, due in Abu Dhabi next week. A UN panel has separately concluded that Russia is committing crimes against humanity by targeting civilians in Ukraine, a finding Moscow has generally rejected.

The outcome of the Abu Dhabi talks remains uncertain, and the continued strikes on rescue operations and the power grid heading into winter are likely to shape Ukraine's negotiating position.

stories.headline: Update: Miller Appointment Signals Limited Cooperation With Democrats as Congress Returns
stories.summary:
Bloomberg analysts said President Donald Trump's decision to name Stephen Miller White House chief of staff signals he is unlikely to seek significant cooperation with Democrats following their midterm victories. Bloomberg Opinion columnist Gautam Mukunda argued the election results could sharpen partisan divisions while pressuring congressional Republicans to decide how closely to align with the president.

Miller replaces Susie Wiles, a change announced after Republican losses in the midterms. Democrats are set to take power in Congress in January and have said they plan unified, sustained oversight of the administration.

Analysts also discussed the policy terrain ahead. Bloomberg's Shawn Donnan said Trump's midterm rebuke does not mean the end of economic populism, arguing Democrats succeeded by recasting their message around affordability and taking on powerful economic interests. Former strategists from both parties, Republican Leslie Shedd and Democrat John McCarthy, said both sides are recalibrating, with leadership fights and affordability pressure shaping what Congress can accomplish before the change in power.

Supporters of Trump's choice view Miller as a loyal executor of the president's agenda, while critics see the move as a signal of confrontation. The coming weeks will show whether lame-duck negotiations produce any bipartisan action.

stories.headline: Update: Pope Leo Draws 40,000 to First Mass in South America, Urges 'Bridges of Fraternity'
stories.summary:
Pope Leo XIV urged Uruguayans on Saturday to build bridges of fraternity and faith during his first full day in the country, the opening stop of a three-nation South American tour that also includes Argentina and Peru. The Vatican said 40,000 people attended his first Mass in Paysandú, in western Uruguay, despite morning rain.

The trip was in doubt after the pope underwent lung cancer surgery on Oct. 13. Speaking in Spanish, Leo said the Catholic faith has been part of Uruguayan life since its earliest days and must be passed on to future generations "with creative courage." He invoked the nearby bridge over the Uruguay River to Argentina and praised the ritual of sharing mate tea as a symbol of unity.

He also visited a Catholic university and a violence-ravaged Montevideo neighborhood where church groups have built homes, provided jobs and run drug rehabilitation programs. The visit aims to raise the profile of the church in Uruguay, the region's most secular country, where even Catholic holidays carry secular names.

The 12-day tour continues to Argentina and Peru, and his health during the demanding schedule will be closely watched.

stories.headline: Update: Paraguay's Former President Peña Charged Over Ueno Bank Collapse
stories.summary:
Prosecutors in Paraguay have formally charged former president Santiago Peña over his alleged role in the banking scandal that led to his impeachment. He is accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain. Peña denies any wrongdoing, and his defense lawyer, Ricardo Preda, called the allegations a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic."

Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including members of his own party, voted unanimously to remove him following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has ties to his private business interests. The Senate vote was 44 in favor, with one lawmaker absent. Peña had offered to resign, but senators impeached him instead, stripping him of the immunity usually granted to former presidents. The charges alleged conflicts of interest, manipulation of regulatory oversight, diversion of pension funds, and participation in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

The bank's seizure by the central bank left an estimated three million depositors unable to reach their savings and pensions, more than half of the country's population. Long lines formed at Ueno branches in Asuncion, and protests spread nationwide, with some clashes in which police used tear gas and water cannons. Senator Rafael Filizzola called it "the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history."

Pedro Alliana, Peña's deputy, has been sworn in as interim president and will serve until 2028. He pledged that affected depositors "will be fully compensated." Analysts expect further prosecution of Peña over the bank's collapse.

stories.headline: Update: Krakow Gunman Named Victims Include His Parents and Sister
stories.summary:
Polish police confirmed on Sunday that the three bodies found at the Krakow gunman's home were his 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 21-year-old sister. The discovery came when police searched the house after the attack in Krakow's Main Market Square. Prime Minister Donald Tusk had earlier said two women and one man were found there.

In the square, the gunman drove in and fired at random people from his car shortly before 15:00 local time. Six people were killed there: four Poles, a British national and an Austrian woman. Sixteen people, including five foreigners, two police officers and the attacker, were taken to hospital. The injured came from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

Armed officers shot the suspect within three minutes of the attack beginning, which officials said prevented a larger massacre. One of the two injured officers was shot three times while making the arrest and is in very critical condition, a government minister said. Tusk named the officers as Senior Constable Jakub Kulik and Senior Constable Artur Moranski.

The 25-year-old suspect remains in hospital after surgery for a gunshot wound. The Krakow branch of the National Public Prosecutor's Office has opened an investigation into what it described as a terrorist offence, and authorities say the suspect is believed to have far-right ties. The suspect's car was checked for explosives and none were found.

stories.headline: Update: US Task Force Iron Gate Targets Iran's Land and Caspian Weapons Routes as IRGC Announces Underground Production Plans
stories.summary:
US Central Command announced Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday, a unit meant to stop Iran from moving advanced weapons and other materials across its land borders and the Caspian Sea. It extends the existing naval blockade of Iranian ports. Based in Tampa, Florida, it will reportedly be staffed by about 20 civilian and military personnel and coordinate with other US agencies on dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illegal revenue streams.

CENTCOM Commander Admiral Brad Cooper said the unit will reinforce the success of the blockade at sea. Iran borders seven countries: Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkiye and Turkmenistan. Michael Mulroy, a former US deputy assistant defense secretary, told Al Jazeera that if President Trump escalates, targets would likely be economic and infrastructure sites rather than the military targets of Operation Epic Fury.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded the same day by announcing plans for underground complexes capable of sustaining missile and drone production under bombardment. This followed reports, based on satellite imagery, of construction near Iranian missile bases. IRGC spokesman Sardar Mohebi dismissed the task force as "just a play on words" and noted that Washington had earlier predicted Iran's economic collapse within two weeks, which did not occur.

Analysts say the unit could also disrupt supply networks linking Iran and Russia, though CENTCOM did not say so explicitly. The moves come as concern grows about a renewed war.

stories.headline: Update: New Zealand's Tight Election Leaves Centrist Opportunity Party With Balance of Power
stories.summary:
New Zealand's election produced no clear winner. A record number of voters deserted the two major parties, and the result will likely take weeks to resolve into a governing coalition. Gains came for the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party.

The Opportunity Party, which had never won a seat before, now holds seven and could decide who governs. Leader Quilae Wong told supporters on election night: "You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good." Coalition negotiations will determine the next prime minister.

The vote took place amid unusually low national morale. Polling shows more than half of New Zealanders no longer see the country as a land of opportunity, and a record number are emigrating. Unemployment is at an 11-year high and rising, and about one in three people under 24 cannot find enough work or have none.

Voters interviewed by the BBC described apathy and disillusionment, and some said they did not vote at all. Whoever forms the government will inherit a weak economy, high living costs and eroding public faith in politics.

stories.headline: Sotomayor Says She Hopes Supreme Court Will Overturn Presidential Immunity Ruling
stories.summary:
Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor said Saturday that she hopes the court's decision granting former presidents broad criminal immunity will be overturned, saying her colleagues have done some "crazy things." She spoke at a civics education event at George Washington's Mount Vernon estate. It was the first time she had publicly commented on the matter in this way.

Asked how hopeful she is about the rule of law, Sotomayor said the country is going through a "rough patch," referring to the state of rule of law and civic discourse. The remarks drew coverage from more than two dozen outlets across the political spectrum, in part because of the political moment. Democrats won the Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, which will make it harder for President Trump, who nominated three justices in his first term, to confirm a nominee if a vacancy arises.

Pressure has grown on conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito to retire, though neither has shown any sign of imminently stepping down. Many conservatives view the loss of both chambers of Congress as a setback for their judicial ambitions, while some liberal commentators have urged older justices to act with their legacies in mind. Critics of Sotomayor's remarks may view public comments from a sitting justice on a decided case as unusual, while supporters see them as a candid defense of the rule of law.

The Supreme Court is also weighing whether to hear a case on bans on AR-15 style rifles. Democrats, now preparing to take control of the Senate, have signaled they could reshape how Trump's judicial and other nominations proceed.

stories.headline: Update: Krakow Gunman Who Killed 6 Has Far-Right Views, Polish Authorities Say
stories.summary:
A 25-year-old Polish man drove into Krakow's Main Square on Saturday and opened fire with an automatic weapon, killing six people and injuring 15 others before police shot and wounded him. The square is a major tourist destination in Poland's second-largest city. Armed police responded, and two nearby schools went into lockdown.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said the suspect was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held "very radical views," and described him as a likely domestic far-right extremist. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the attack an act of terrorism. The suspect, a Polish citizen, has been arrested.

A previous report noted that three bodies were later found at the attacker's home, and a British citizen is among the dead. The new development is the authorities' identification of the suspect's ideological motivations and his age. The attack has intensified scrutiny of extremism in Poland, where the political climate is already tense amid disputes between the government and President Karol Nawrocki.

Investigators are expected to examine how the suspect obtained an automatic weapon and whether he had contacts with extremist networks. Authorities have not yet released further details on his background or on the condition of all those wounded.

stories.headline: Update: US Military Fires on Cargo Ship in Gulf of Oman Enforcing Iran Blockade
stories.summary:
A U.S. military aircraft fired on and disabled a St. Kitts-flagged commercial cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday, U.S. Central Command said. CENTCOM said the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to breach a naval blockade on Iran. The incident marks a new escalation in the ongoing conflict with Iran.

Separately, CENTCOM announced Task Force Iron Gate, a new unit designed to block Iranian ground transit routes, including across the Caspian Sea, used to move advanced weapons, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue. The task force will work with other U.S. agencies. U.S. officials did not say whether military action would be used to stop shipments entering Iran by land.

The Associated Press also reported that President Trump said the U.S. has carried out new limited strikes on Iran targeting air defense systems, while Iran's leaders weigh proposals. Iranian state media reported blasts on Qeshm Island and in Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas. Trump launched major combat operations against Iran on Feb. 28.

The conflict has become a political issue at home. Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the decision to start the war, while some Republicans and Democrats have questioned it after the midterms, and Vice President JD Vance has been reported to be pushing behind the scenes for a ceasefire and nuclear talks.

stories.headline: Strong Earthquake Shakes Central Japan, Injuring at Least 22
stories.summary:
A magnitude 5.7 earthquake, as measured by the Japan Meteorological Agency, struck central Japan at 1:04 a.m. Sunday, injuring at least 22 people, according to local media. The U.S. Geological Survey put the magnitude at 5.5. The quake was centered about 25 miles below the surface in Shizuoka Prefecture.

The strongest shaking was recorded in neighboring Aichi Prefecture, and a wide area was affected, including Hamamatsu, Kyoto, Nara, Gifu and Yamanashi, home to Mount Fuji. Television footage showed shattered store windows and glass on streets, and a bookstore with books thrown from shelves. Some injuries occurred when people fell on stairs while fleeing buildings. The quake was not felt in Tokyo.

The weather agency warned of possible strong quakes in the coming week, especially over the next two to three days, and urged vigilance for mudslides and falling rocks. An agency official, Ayataka Ebita, said no apparent change had been detected on the Nankai Trough plate boundary, where scientists say a megaquake could occur. Shinkansen bullet trains ran at reduced speeds as a precaution.
